- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to compensate for downward bias.
- If model shows sharp upward spike followed by forecast overshoot, apply a “lag correction”: reduce forecast by 5–10% in the following 2–3 periods.
- If model consistently forecasts higher than true outcome over 3+ consecutive days, apply mean reversion: subtract 0.5–1.5% per day from forecast until convergence.
- For 30-day horizon, if sentiment is neutral or mixed, model often overfits recent volatility; use 10–15% smoothing on forecast to dampen noise.
- If true outcome shows strong upward trend (e.g., >+2% per day), model often fails to capture momentum; adjust forecast upward by 1–2% per day until trend stabilizes.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “reversal” patterns (e.g., bullish → bearish → bullish), model tends to lag; add 1–2 days of lead time in forecast to anticipate sentiment shift.
